questions.q: Identify neutral complex from following.
questions.solution:
Identifying a neutral complex requires calculating the total charge of each coordination entity. The overall charge is the sum of the central metal's oxidation state and the charges from all ligands.

For tetracyanonickelate(II) ion, the nickel center is Ni2+ and four CN– ligands contribute –4, yielding a –2 charge: $+2 + 4 \times (-1) = -2$, an anion.

Sodium hexafluoroaluminate(III) contains the complex ion [AlF6]3–, as aluminum is +3 and six F– ligands contribute –6: $+3 + 6 \times (-1) = -3$, an anion.

Triamminetrinitrocobalt(III) has cobalt at +3, three neutral NH3 ligands, and three NO2– ligands contributing –3: $+3 + 3 \times 0 + 3 \times (-1) = 0$, a neutral complex.

Tetraamminecopper(II) ion features Cu2+ and four neutral NH3 ligands: $+2 + 4 \times 0 = +2$, a cation.

$\boxed{C}$ is the neutral complex.

questions.q: A hollow charged metal sphere has radius ' $R$ '. If the potential difference between its surface and a point at a distance ' $5 \mathrm{R}$ ' from the centre is V, then magnitude of electric field Intensity at a distance ' $5 \mathrm{R}$ ' from the centre of sphere is

questions.q:
A uniformly charged semicircular arc of radius ' $r$ ' has linear charge density $(\lambda)$. What is the electric field at its centre?
( $\epsilon_0=$ permittivity of free space)
questions.solution:
Electric field due to a circular arc at its center,
$\mathrm{E}=\frac{2 \mathrm{k} \lambda}{\mathrm{r}} \sin \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle which arc subtends at its center
For semicircle, $\alpha=90^{\circ}$
Hence, $E=\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_0 r}$

questions.q: A particle at rest starts moving with a constant angular acceleration of $4 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2$ in a circular path. At what time the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration and tangential acceleration will be equal
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \alpha=4 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\ & \text { Centripetal (radial) acceleration, } \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{r} \omega^2 \\ & \text { Tangential acceleration, } \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{r} \alpha \\ & \text { If } \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{t}} \text {, then } \mathrm{r} \omega^2=\mathrm{r} \alpha \\ & \omega=\sqrt{\alpha}=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \omega=\omega_0+\alpha \mathrm{t}=0+\alpha \mathrm{t}=\alpha \mathrm{t} \\ & \text { or } \mathrm{t}=\frac{\omega}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2} \sec \end{aligned}$
